item.title: Surface Design Association: Artist in Residence 2026-27 (virtual)
item.description:
Organisation: Surface Design Association (SDA)

Location: Fully virtual. Open to US-based and international applicants; current SDA membership is required.

Award: $2,000 studio stipend, plus up to $2,000 further compensation for programming work (SDA aims for roughly $4,000 in total per resident). No application fee, but applicants must be current SDA members (membership from $85 per year, $60 for students).

Duration: One year, virtual, October 2026 to August 2027

Deadline: 14 Aug 2026

The Surface Design Association's Artist in Residence programme is built to develop skills, open up relationships and support fiber and textile artists through a studio project that pushes their practice. The residency is entirely virtual and runs across a full year, which is the point: it removes the travel, housing and time-away barriers that keep many practitioners out of in-person residencies. One artist is selected annually by a panel of SDA staff, board members and committee volunteers. WHAT IT INVOLVES: studio visits across the year, social media programming, and meetings with the SDA community, plus further programming shaped around the resident's own skills and interests, which can include teaching online workshops, contributing to SDA publications, jurying exhibitions or joining panels. FUNDING: a $2,000 studio stipend for the project, plus up to $2,000 in additional compensation for programming work, targeting about $4,000 total. ELIGIBILITY: emerging, mid-career and established artists; US-based and international applicants welcome; students and professionals may apply; applicants must hold current SDA membership (from $85 per year, $60 for students). APPLICATION: a portfolio of 10 images with full artwork information (title, year, materials, technique, dimensions, photo credit), a detailed CV, essay responses on artistic goals, programming interests and professional development, and demographic information. No application fee. The 2026-27 cycle closes 14 August 2026.

item.title: Andy Warhol Foundation: Exhibition Support (Fall 2026 round)
item.description:
Organisation: The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts

Location: Applicant's own venue. US-based 501(c)(3) required; international organisations must first submit a letter of inquiry before any proposal is accepted.

Award: USD 60,000 to 100,000. Direct costs only (artist payments, catalogue and publication, artist-designed public programmes); staff salaries excluded. Request must not exceed 25 percent of total direct project costs, which functions as a de facto 75 percent co-financing requirement. No application fee.

Duration: Exhibition must open between 6 months and 2 years after notification.

Deadline: 01 Sep 2026

Supports solo, two-person and thematic group exhibitions of contemporary visual art. The Foundation explicitly prioritises artists whose work is under-recognised and whose practices are experimental or hard to categorise, which makes it a genuine route for media arts, digital culture and art-and-science exhibitions rather than a blue-chip-only fund. Grants of USD 60,000 to 100,000 cover direct exhibition costs including artist fees, new commissions, catalogue production and artist-designed public programming, but not staff salaries. Applicants may request no more than 25 percent of total direct costs. The proposal is a roughly three-page curatorial letter plus detailed direct-cost budget, organisational budget and IRS documentation. Deadlines are 1 March and 1 September annually, with notifications 1 July and 1 January. IMPORTANT: this is a postmark or email-timestamp deadline, not a portal deadline. Fiscal sponsors are explicitly not accepted; the applicant must hold its own IRS ruling letter. The six-month-to-two-year timing rule is strict, so a September 2026 application suits exhibitions programmed from mid-2027 onward.

item.title: Andy Warhol Foundation: Multi-year Program Support (Fall 2026 round)
item.description:
Organisation: The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts

Location: Programming delivered by the applicant organisation. US 501(c)(3) required; international organisations must submit a letter of inquiry first.

Award: USD 60,000 to 100,000 across two years. Request must not exceed 25 percent of the organisation's annual operating budget. No formal match, but the 25 percent cap means the balance must come from elsewhere. No application fee.

Duration: Two years of programming, beginning after the 1 January 2027 notification.

Deadline: 01 Sep 2026

This is the closest thing in US foundation philanthropy to core support for an organisation running an ongoing public programme, as opposed to a single exhibition. It funds a two-year slate of exhibitions, residencies, public art, screenings, performances, lectures and publications, which means a recurring festival or convening series can be underwritten here. Grants are USD 60,000 to 100,000 over two years and may not exceed 25 percent of annual operating budget. The Foundation states a preference for organisations supporting artists with experimental, hard-to-categorise practices, putting digital culture, sound art and art-and-science programmers squarely in scope. Applications require a forward programme schedule covering at least the twelve months after the award, a three-page narrative focused specifically on how artists benefit (the stated central evaluation criterion), a full one-year organisational budget and 501(c)(3) documentation. Deadlines are 1 March and 1 September, notifications 1 July and 1 January. Fiscal sponsors are not accepted. Organisations that received a Multi-year grant within the past year are ineligible, and proposals centred on anniversaries, relocations or major renovations are explicitly discouraged.

item.title: Paul Hamlyn Foundation: Arts-based Learning Fund (rolling)
item.description:
Organisation: Paul Hamlyn Foundation

Location: United Kingdom. Activity must take place with UK state-funded schools, SEND specialist schools, FE colleges or alternative provision settings.

Award: GBP 30,000 to 300,000 total, capped at GBP 100,000 per year. Covers project costs and associated core and overhead costs of arts-education partnership work. No stated co-financing requirement. No application fee.

Duration: 1 to 4 years.

Deadline: Rolling / undated

The Arts-based Learning Fund supports sustained partnerships between arts and cultural organisations and state-funded educational settings so that arts-based approaches become embedded in how young people learn. Grants run GBP 30,000 to 300,000 over one to four years, with a ceiling of GBP 100,000 in any single year, and can cover both project delivery and a fair share of the applicant's core costs. Applicants must be arts and cultural organisations (charities, community organisations, social enterprises, not-for-profits) applying in partnership with at least one state-funded educational setting. Applications are accepted on a rolling basis with no deadlines; an optional enquiry call with a grants manager is encouraged before applying. The process is two-stage: an initial online application, then, if shortlisted, further information plus a phone or video conversation, with a final decision by a grants panel. TIMING RULE: applicants should expect a response within about four months, and successful applicants should allow roughly six months from application to receiving funds, so projects should not be planned to start sooner than that. The Foundation explicitly encourages applications from organisations led by people most impacted by racism, ableism, classism, sexism, xenophobia, homophobia and transphobia. IMPORTANT: this is the only Paul Hamlyn arts route open to new applicants in 2026, since the main Arts Fund is suspended to new applications until at least April 2027.

item.title: Creative Scotland: National Lottery Open Fund for Organisations (rolling)
item.description:
Organisation: Creative Scotland

Location: Activity must take place in Scotland and benefit people in Scotland. Applicant organisations must be constituted and based in Scotland; organisations elsewhere in the UK with a UK-wide remit may apply for activity in Scotland; organisations outside the UK must have a UK-based partner lead the application.

Award: GBP 1,000 to 100,000. Covers a one-off project or production, creative research and development, a longer-term programme of work, or business and organisational development. No stated match-funding requirement and no application fee. Applicants must hold a UK bank account in the same name as the application.

Duration: Projects or programmes lasting up to 18 months.

Deadline: Rolling / undated

The National Lottery Open Fund for Organisations is Creative Scotland's main open-access grant for constituted arts, creative and cultural organisations, and it is genuinely rolling with no deadlines. It supports a specific one-off project or production, creative research and development, or a longer-term programme of work, and can also fund business sustainability and organisational development costs. Eligible organisations can apply for GBP 1,000 to 100,000 for projects lasting up to 18 months. TIMING RULES: decision lag is banded by request size, with GBP 1,000 to 20,000 decided within 10 weeks and GBP 20,000 to 100,000 within 14 weeks. The start date must be after the decision date, and the guidance recommends allowing a further 2 to 4 weeks for funding agreements and first payment. Critically for festivals, applicants are barred from starting activity, including advertising events or issuing calls for collaborators, before funding is confirmed, so a public programme should be planned to start roughly 12 to 18 weeks after submission. Only one application may be in assessment at any time. Non-UK organisations can be involved but cannot lead. Current Regularly Funded and Multi-Year Funded Organisations are excluded.

item.title: Esmee Fairbairn Foundation: Community-led Art and Creativity (rolling)
item.description:
Organisation: Esmee Fairbairn Foundation

Location: United Kingdom. Work must directly benefit communities in the UK.

Award: GBP 30,000 minimum, no maximum. Funds core costs or project costs including staff salaries and overheads; unrestricted funding available to charities. No co-financing requirement stated. No application fee.

Duration: No formal minimum or maximum, but most grants run three to five years.

Deadline: Rolling / undated

Community-led Art and Creativity sits within Esmee Fairbairn's Creative, Confident Communities aim and is one of the Foundation's two arts-related priorities. It funds work where local people and local artists lead the creative and cultural activity in a place, emphasising cross-sector collaboration that delivers social, environmental and economic benefit alongside artistic outcomes. Cited examples include the Migration Museum's People's Panel, B Arts in Stoke and WeCanMake's Festival of Making Together, which confirms festivals and public programmes are in scope where genuinely community-directed. Applications are rolling with no deadlines, starting with an eligibility quiz and an expression of interest. The minimum grant is GBP 30,000 with no upper limit, and most awards run three to five years covering core or project costs including salaries and overheads. Applicants need at least GBP 100,000 annual turnover in the latest accounts and a formal constitution, charitable or non-charitable so long as the work is charitable. This is highly competitive: in 2025 only around 5 percent of initial expressions of interest converted into funded grants, so long-term systems-change framing matters more than the individual event. Esmee's other arts priority, Arts and Creativity Making Change, is currently closed.

Residency programme run by the Institut francais de Paris with the Cite internationale des arts, one of France's largest international artist mobility programmes, supporting nearly seventy artists and cultural professionals each year. The Institut francais covers the monthly cost of the studio; the artist's nominating partner organisation submits the application and must provide a stipend of at least EUR 1,100 per month plus international travel, insurance and visa fees. ELIGIBILITY: established artists and cultural professionals of any nationality who have lived outside France for at least 5 years, with an active professional practice, a clearly defined research or creative project, and professional-level French and/or English; open across disciplines (theatre, dance, performance, visual arts, music, literature, cinema, architecture, design, digital creation, photography, fashion, crafts, curating, and more). GLINA3 is an Amsterdam clay 3D printing and digital design studio, and it is looking for one collaborator to join a new research project at the intersection of typography, language, technology and material culture. They want an artist, writer, poet, anthropologist or artistic researcher whose existing practice already engages with type design, typography, writing systems, visual language, fonts and letterforms, language technologies, or the tools that shape how language is produced, read or translated. This is an unusually good fit for anyone working on the machine-readable side of language: the brief explicitly names language technologies and translation tooling alongside classical type design. ELIGIBILITY: individual practitioners with demonstrable work in one or more of the listed areas. HOW TO APPLY: the studio asks for relevant work, research, publications or projects connected to type, fonts, writing systems, visual language or the tools that shape them, and nothing else. Because the deadline is tight they say Instagram DM is the fastest route; you can also email a short introduction and one relevant project to office@glina3.nl. item.title: transmediale x Pro Helvetia Digital Art Residency 2027
item.description:
Organisation: transmediale (in cooperation with the Swiss Arts Council Pro Helvetia)

Location: Hybrid: remote plus on-site at transmediale studio, silent green Kulturquartier, Berlin-Wedding, Germany. RESTRICTED: applicants must hold Swiss nationality or permanent residence in Switzerland and be firmly established in the Swiss cultural scene (Pro Helvetia's general requirements apply).

Award: Artist fee of CHF 2,000 per month across the two-month residency (CHF 4,000), plus a production grant of CHF 15,000 for the selected project, plus travel and accommodation for both the festival and the residency month. Duos and collectives may apply but the fee and the production grant stay the same and must be shared. No application fee.

Duration: Two-month hybrid residency between mid-May and mid-July 2027, with the whole of June 2027 on-site in Berlin (mandatory)

Deadline: 28 Aug 2026

The fifth iteration of transmediale's Digital Art Residency, run with the Swiss Arts Council Pro Helvetia, awarded to one individual or collective working in digital art practices at the intersection of media arts, performance, sound and moving image. THEME: the 2027 programme sits under transmediale's 40th-anniversary framework RFC 40, named after the early internet Request for Comments series, and treats the festival as a counter-infrastructure: the call asks how a network stays legible to itself while surrounding structures break down, and how technical paradigms can be reconfigured into new cultural protocols outside extractive logics, moving from critique to construction. Proposals should offer alternatives to how we understand, respond to and shape the technological conditions we inhabit. WHAT IS OFFERED: an artist fee of CHF 2,000 per month for two months; a CHF 15,000 production grant supporting a new work or the continuation of an existing project, open to all formats and building on the research begun during the residency (the project must be completed by December 2027 at the latest); travel and accommodation for the festival and the residency; a shared modular working space at transmediale studio; connections to Berlin institutions and stakeholders; a public presentation in transmediale's year-round studio programme; and the option of an online publication in transmediale's journal. STRUCTURE: kick-off with a presentation of the residency projects during transmediale 2027 (26 to 31 January 2027, attendance optional but strongly recommended); onboarding and the first hybrid stretch in May 2027; the mandatory on-site month in Berlin in June 2027; and a second hybrid stretch including reporting in July 2027. Availability for the festival week and for the whole of June in Berlin are treated as key prerequisites. TIMELINE: open call 16 July to 28 August 2026 (23:59 CEST); selected residents announced October 2026. Applications are only accepted via transmediale's submission forms. item.title: Privacy Camp 2026 (EDRi): Call for Sessions, The Origins of Future Technologies
item.description:
Organisation: European Digital Rights (EDRi), with LSTS at Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Privacy Salon vzw, the Institute for European Studies at Université Saint-Louis Bruxelles, and the Racism and Technology Center

Location: Brussels, Belgium, and online (hybrid). Event on 13 October 2026.

Award: NO speaker fee or honorarium. Where needed, up to EUR 400 per speaker or session organiser towards transport to and accommodation in Brussels, reimbursed against invoices and travel tickets; those with organisational support are encouraged to cover their own expenses. No budget beyond this cap. Free to propose and free to attend (registration open).

Duration: One-day conference on 13 October 2026. Average session length 50 minutes.

Deadline: Closed 10 Aug 2026

Privacy Camp holds its 14th edition on 13 October 2026 in Brussels and online, organised by European Digital Rights (EDRi) with the Research Group on Law, Science, Technology & Society (LSTS) at Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Privacy Salon vzw, the Institute for European Studies at Université Saint-Louis Bruxelles, and the Racism and Technology Center. THEME: 'The Origins of Future Technologies: Towards communities of digital self-determination'. The call starts from the premise that digital futures do not appear from nowhere but are built through land, labour, capital, infrastructure, law, public money, political choices and social struggle, and asks where technologies come from, who gets to shape them, and what conditions make digital self-determination possible. It situates this against the EU's 2026 Tech Sovereignty Package (semiconductors, artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure and data centres) and the wider deregulatory agenda including the Digital Omnibus, the AI Omnibus and reforms affecting data protection, privacy, labour and environmental safeguards, asking whose version of sovereignty is actually being discussed. TOPIC AREAS: (1) Material conditions in the production of technologies, covering the natural resources needed across the supply chain (critical components such as semiconductors, water for data centres) and how GDPR, ePrivacy and AI Act safeguards shape the material conditions of AI from data extraction and biometric processing through to data centres, labour and public infrastructure; labour conditions, including who mines critical materials, union-busting across the tech supply chain, and coalitions between tech workers, unions, migrant justice groups, climate movements and digital rights organisations; and capital, meaning the venture capital forces driving the current AI hype and consolidating through defence, security and militarisation. (2) Political vision in the use of technologies, covering military use and how militarisation and securitisation shape the EU deregulation debate, and the political ideologies driving technology development, including what digital self-determination means for communities facing racialised discrimination, surveillance, occupation, border violence, workplace control or environmental harm. (3) Moving technologies forward through communities, covering community innovation for digital self-determination (distributed and self-hosted data storage, AI built by and for community needs, community-led, public or cooperative digital infrastructure); law, deregulation and rights (resisting the Digital Omnibus and specifically the Data Omnibus, defending GDPR and ePrivacy safeguards, protecting access, transparency and automated decision-making rights, enforcing existing digital laws, supporting collective litigation, and challenging the framing of rights as obstacles to EU competitiveness); and building power by connecting grassroots movements across tech worker organising, labour, migrant, LGBTQIA+, climate, economic justice and landback movements. FORMATS: interactive workshops are particularly encouraged, meaning small-group work, peer exchange and collaboration across sectors, coalitions and disciplines, moving from talk to strategic action; panel discussions are also welcome, especially those centring diverse voices and grounded lived experience with room for meaningful audience engagement. SUBMISSION GUIDELINES: state a clear objective for the session and what a good outcome would be; make it as interactive as possible; support a diversity of voices and multiple perspectives; average session length is 50 minutes; propose the format that actually suits the idea rather than forcing a panel into a workshop or vice versa. For workshops, make the objectives, structure and facilitation clear and have participants work together in small groups towards a specific goal; the organisers provide additional guidance, support and feedback for workshops. For panels, list a maximum of 4 speakers covering academia, civil society and decision-maker perspectives, and indicate which speakers have confirmed at least in principle. TIMELINE: proposals due via the online form by 10 August 2026 at 09:00 CEST; the Content Committee notifies applicants before 21 August 2026; confirmation to proceed required by 25 August; draft programme published 4 September; speakers and final session description confirmed by 10 September at the latest (earlier confirmation improves the odds that the EUR 400 reimbursement budget covers speaker travel and accommodation); final programme published 28 September. The 2026 Content Committee is Andreea Belu (EDRi), Gloria González Fuster (LSTS, VUB), Jill Toh (Racism and Technology Center), Sanne Stevens (Justice, Equity and Technology Project) and Alexandra Giannopoulou (DFF). item.title: Alliance for Gender Equality in Europe: Strengthening Movements for Gender Equality (2026 call)
item.description:
Organisation: Alliance for Gender Equality in Europe (hosted by the Network of European Foundations)

Location: European Union, United Kingdom, Armenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Serbia. All coalition partners must be based and operating in these countries.

Award: EUR 2,700,000 total across the call. Between EUR 225,000 and EUR 450,000 per grant over 3 years (EUR 75,000 to EUR 150,000 per year). Project support including salary and overhead costs; overheads capped at 20 percent. 6 to 12 coalitions expected to be funded. Free to apply.

Duration: 3 years, January 2027 to December 2029. Renewal possible at the end of the cycle subject to budget.

Deadline: Closed 07 Aug 2026

NOTE: this is a gender-equality movement-building fund rather than an arts or technology programme, and it is coalition-only (no individual applicants). Relevance to creative or tech practice runs through the narrative-change and digital-storytelling strand of the call. The Alliance for Gender Equality in Europe, a philanthropic initiative created in 2021 and hosted by the Network of European Foundations, is launching an open call under its forthcoming Strengthening Movements Fund. The Alliance is composed of the Bodossaki Foundation, Fondation BNP Paribas, Fondation CHANEL, Fondazione con il Sud, Fondation de France, Fondation RAJA-Danièle Marcovici, King Baudouin Foundation and L'Oréal Fund for Women; this particular fund is backed by all of those except Fondation BNP Paribas. OBJECTIVE: to foster collaboration and solidarity within European intersectional and grassroots movements so that they can collectively advance gender equality in Europe in the long term. The call follows a 2025 Alliance-commissioned mapping of European gender-equality movements (30 in-depth interviews plus contextual research) which found movements under-resourced because philanthropic funding frameworks are misaligned with their needs; the fund is designed to replace short-term reactive funding with proactive long-term support. OUTCOMES SOUGHT: community organising reinforced at local or national level; pan-European feminist collaborations and solidarity strengthened; alliances between gender equality and other social justice movements expanded; pro-gender-equality narratives and voices amplified in local, national, regional or digital spaces; policy debates informed by feminist and gender equality movements. ELIGIBLE ACTIVITIES INCLUDE (non-exhaustive): national, regional or pan-European convenings and collaborative projects where groups co-create joint strategies; joint campaigns between feminist movements and allied movements (climate justice, anti-racism, LGBTQI+, disability rights); narrative-change training for grassroots groups covering framing, messaging, digital tools and digital storytelling; cross-border coalitions advocating EU institutions or national governments; facilitated virtual or in-person convenings to work through internal tensions and build trust; translating academic research on anti-gender efforts into movement strategies. ELIGIBILITY: collective proposals with at least 3 organisations per coalition (no maximum); legally registered non-profits (NGOs, civil society organisations, social enterprises, national or regional funds); based and operating in the target countries; small and medium grassroots organisations, defined by annual budget under EUR 450,000 (Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Sweden, UK) or under EUR 300,000 (Armenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Republic of Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Kosovo, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Serbia). Intermediary organisations and networks are exempt from the budget thresholds but must apply in coalition with grassroots organisations, with the budget fairly distributed among all partners. Coalitions must be community-led (majority of leadership roles held by members of the community supported, and/or participatory approaches), work with marginalised women, transgender, non-binary and gender non-conforming people, use gender transformative approaches, and hold an intersectional perspective. Proposals must be completed in English. Each organisation may submit only one application, as lead or as partner. One organisation per coalition acts as lead, is the primary contact and is legally responsible for the grant; leads are invited to networking, peer-learning and capacity-strengthening activities. SCORING (100 points): relevance to the call objective 20; demonstrated track record in strengthening movements 20 (learnings valued as well as achievements); strong impact 25 (must contribute to at least one of the five outcomes, with clear measurement); ability to work collaboratively and inclusively with partners 20 (including fair budget repartition); quality and feasibility 15. PROCESS: two stages. Stage 1 opened 29 June 2026 and closes 7 August 2026 at 23:59 CEST, submitted in English via the online platform (a PDF of the form is downloadable for reference only). Pre-selection results by email 14 September 2026; stage 2 runs 16 September to 23 October 2026 and includes due-diligence contact from Alliance staff; final results by email in December 2026; grants start January 2027. The Alliance is piloting a participatory selection process for this call, with grant-making decisions made jointly by a committee of funders and non-funders holding equal decision-making power. item.description:

The Good Life Residents Program is a six-month Roosevelt Institute initiative that develops new leaders and elevates bold ideas across six economic policy priorities under its Good Life Agenda. Each topic area hosts a cohort of 3 to 4 residents plus 1 to 2 senior Topic Advisors (academics, policy leaders, organizers or government practitioners) who provide strategic and intellectual mentorship and moderate the closing event. Residents write a roughly 1,500-word original policy essay advancing a people-centered policy vision against a topic-specific prompt, take part in structured dialogue with peers, Topic Advisors and Roosevelt Think Tank directors, help prepare and appear at a culminating public event, contribute to press opportunities such as op-eds and reporter calls where applicable, and act as ambassadors for the Good Life Agenda in their professional and public networks. The current round, the AI and Finance Residents Program, is run in partnership with Data & Society and asks for bold ideas on how to shape, redirect, interrupt or make more visible and contestable the flows of capital into generative AI. Framing: breakneck investment in generative AI technology and infrastructure is distorting the stock market, profit measures, bond issuance, the pace and composition of growth, job creation and trade policy, with seven tech companies accounting for more than a third of S&P 500 market capitalisation and complex, sometimes circular financial arrangements obscuring risk. Suggested lines of inquiry include what government interventions could improve public oversight, risk allocation and direction-setting in private markets; how other investments could be coordinated and scaled if AI spending is crowding them out; what role public spending or new institutions could play in catalysing technology R&D designed to support workers, sustainability and supply chains; what democratic input mechanisms would keep state influence over capital flows less vulnerable to corruption; and how federal AI policy should address public hostility to data centre investments alongside national security and competitiveness. Compensation is USD 3,000 plus travel and accommodation for the culminating event.
